topics.name: Java Basics
topics.description: Program structure, primitive types, variables, operators and console output.
keyPoints: Every Java program starts at public static void main(String[] args) inside a class.
Primitive types (int, double, boolean, char, long) hold values directly; String is a class, not a primitive.
Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 is 3, while 7 / 2.0 is 3.5.

topics.name: Control Flow
topics.description: if/else, switch, for, while and do-while loops, break and continue.
keyPoints: if/else chooses a branch; switch selects among constants and needs break (or the arrow syntax) to avoid fall-through.
Use for when the number of iterations is known, while when it depends on a condition, and do-while when the body must run at least once.
break leaves the loop; continue skips to the next iteration.

topics.name: Methods & Arrays
topics.description: Defining methods, parameters, return values, overloading and working with arrays.
keyPoints: Java passes arguments by value: a method gets a copy of a primitive, or a copy of an object reference.
Overloading means the same method name with different parameter lists; the return type alone cannot tell overloads apart.
Array indexes start at 0, the last valid index is length - 1, and an array's size is fixed.

topics.name: Strings & StringBuilder
topics.description: String immutability, common String methods, formatting and StringBuilder.
keyPoints: String objects are immutable: methods such as toUpperCase() return a new String.
Compare String contents with equals(), not ==, which compares references.
Use StringBuilder to build strings in loops; repeated + creates many temporary objects.

topics.name: Classes & Objects
topics.description: Fields, constructors, methods, encapsulation, static members and object references.
keyPoints: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance created with new, and a constructor initializes it.
Encapsulation: keep fields private and expose behavior through public methods.
static members belong to the class itself, not to any single object.

topics.name: Inheritance & Polymorphism
topics.description: extends, method overriding, super, dynamic dispatch and the Object class.
keyPoints: A subclass uses extends to inherit fields and methods; super refers to the parent class.
Overriding replaces a parent method in the subclass; the version that runs depends on the real object type (dynamic dispatch).
Every class extends Object, which provides toString(), equals() and hashCode().

topics.name: Interfaces & Abstract Classes
topics.description: Abstract classes, interfaces, default methods and programming to an interface.
keyPoints: An interface declares what a type can do; a class implements it and can implement many interfaces.
An abstract class can hold state and partial implementation but cannot be instantiated; a class can extend only one class.
Program to an interface (List<String> x = new ArrayList<>()) so implementations can be swapped.

topics.name: Exception Handling
topics.description: try/catch/finally, checked vs unchecked exceptions, try-with-resources, custom exceptions.
keyPoints: Checked exceptions (such as IOException) must be caught or declared; unchecked ones extend RuntimeException.
finally runs whether or not an exception occurs; try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable resources automatically.
Catch specific exceptions first and never swallow them silently.

topics.name: Generics
topics.description: Generic classes and methods, type parameters, bounded types and wildcards.
keyPoints: Generics add compile-time type safety: List<String> only holds Strings, so no casts are needed.
A type parameter such as <T> makes a class or method reusable; a bound like <T extends Number> limits it.
List<Integer> is not a List<Number>; use wildcards such as List<? extends Number> to accept both.

topics.name: Collections Framework
topics.description: List, Set, Map and Queue, ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap, iteration, equals and hashCode.
keyPoints: List keeps order and allows duplicates; Set rejects duplicates; Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys.
HashMap and HashSet need consistent equals() and hashCode(); lookups are O(1) on average.
ArrayList gives fast index access; LinkedList is better only for frequent insertion and removal at the ends.

topics.name: Lambdas & Streams
topics.description: Functional interfaces, lambdas, method references and the Stream API (map, filter, collect).
keyPoints: A lambda is a short implementation of a functional interface (one abstract method), for example x -> x * 2.
Streams process data in a pipeline: a source, intermediate operations (filter, map) and a terminal operation (collect, forEach).
Intermediate stream operations are lazy; nothing runs until a terminal operation is called.

topics.name: Concurrency Basics
topics.description: Threads, ExecutorService, synchronization, thread safety and CompletableFuture.
keyPoints: Threads run concurrently; shared mutable state needs synchronization (synchronized, locks, atomic classes) to avoid race conditions.
Prefer an ExecutorService thread pool to creating threads by hand.
CompletableFuture chains asynchronous steps (supplyAsync, thenApply) without blocking.

topics.name: Command Line Basics
topics.description: Navigating folders, running programs and reading output in a terminal.
keyPoints: pwd shows the current folder, ls (dir on Windows) lists files and cd changes folder.
Commands take arguments and flags, for example ls -l.
The output of one command can be piped into another with |, and > redirects output to a file.

topics.name: Git Basics
topics.description: Repositories, staging, commits, history and pushing to a remote.
keyPoints: git add stages changes; git commit records a snapshot of the staged changes with a message.
git status shows what changed; git log shows the history.
git push sends commits to a remote such as GitHub; git pull fetches and merges remote changes.

topics.name: Branching & Pull Requests
topics.description: Branches, merging, resolving conflicts and reviewing code through pull requests.
keyPoints: A branch is a movable pointer to a line of commits; create one with git switch -c name (or git checkout -b name).
Merging combines branches; a conflict happens when both changed the same lines and must be resolved by hand.
A pull request asks to merge a branch and lets teammates review the change first.

topics.name: Maven & Gradle
topics.description: Build files, dependencies, the build lifecycle and running a Java project from the command line.
keyPoints: Maven uses pom.xml and Gradle uses build.gradle(.kts) to declare dependencies and build steps.
Dependencies are downloaded from repositories such as Maven Central by their coordinates: group, artifact and version.
Typical commands: mvn test and mvn package, or ./gradlew test and ./gradlew build.

topics.name: Relational Databases & SELECT
topics.description: Tables, rows, primary keys and writing basic SELECT queries.
keyPoints: A table has columns and rows; a primary key uniquely identifies each row.
SELECT chooses columns and FROM chooses the table: SELECT name FROM students;
SELECT * returns all columns; in real code list only the columns you need.

topics.name: Filtering, Sorting & Aggregates
topics.description: WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, COUNT/SUM/AVG, GROUP BY and HAVING.
keyPoints: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY.
Aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) collapse rows into one value per group.
ORDER BY sorts (ascending by default); LIMIT restricts the number of rows returned.

topics.name: Joins
topics.description: Foreign keys, INNER and LEFT joins, joining several tables and subqueries.
keyPoints: A foreign key links a row to a row in another table.
INNER JOIN returns only matching rows; LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where there is no match.
Always join on key columns (ON a.id = b.a_id); forgetting the condition creates a huge cross product.

topics.name: Modifying Data & Transactions
topics.description: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, transactions, COMMIT/ROLLBACK and ACID properties.
keyPoints: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes rows and DELETE removes rows; always use WHERE with UPDATE and DELETE.
A transaction groups statements: COMMIT saves them all, ROLLBACK undoes them all.
ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability.

topics.name: Schema Design & Normalization
topics.description: Modelling entities and relationships, one-to-many and many-to-many, normal forms.
keyPoints: One-to-many is modelled with a foreign key on the 'many' side; many-to-many needs a join table.
First normal form: atomic values and no repeating groups. Second and third forms remove partial and transitive dependencies.
Normalization reduces duplication and update anomalies; denormalizing can help read speed.

topics.name: Indexes & Query Performance
topics.description: How indexes work, choosing indexes and reading a query plan.
keyPoints: An index (often a B-tree) lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.
Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY; each index slows INSERT and UPDATE and uses space.
EXPLAIN shows the query plan, for example whether a full table scan or an index scan is used.

topics.name: JDBC
topics.description: Connecting to a database from Java, PreparedStatement, ResultSet and mapping rows to objects.
keyPoints: A Connection opens a session to the database; a Statement runs SQL; a ResultSet iterates over returned rows with next().
Use PreparedStatement with ? placeholders to prevent SQL injection instead of concatenating strings.
Close connections with try-with-resources and map each row to an object by reading columns by name.

topics.name: HTTP Fundamentals
topics.description: Requests and responses, methods, status codes, headers and URLs.
keyPoints: A client sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body); the server returns a response (status code, headers, body).
GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part of a resource and DELETE removes it.
Status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

topics.name: REST API Design
topics.description: Resources, endpoints, idempotency, status codes for APIs and versioning.
keyPoints: REST models things as resources with nouns in URLs (/students/42) and uses HTTP methods as the actions.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating the request leaves the same result; POST is not.
Use meaningful status codes: 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found.

topics.name: JSON & Jackson
topics.description: JSON syntax and converting between JSON and Java objects with Jackson.
keyPoints: JSON has objects {}, arrays [], strings, numbers, booleans and null; keys are double-quoted strings.
Jackson's ObjectMapper converts Java objects to JSON (writeValueAsString) and back (readValue).
Annotations such as @JsonProperty and @JsonIgnore customize field names and visibility.

topics.name: Spring Core & Dependency Injection
topics.description: Inversion of control, beans, the application context and constructor injection.
keyPoints: Inversion of control: the Spring container creates objects (beans) and wires their dependencies for you.
Prefer constructor injection: dependencies are explicit, can be final and are easy to test.
@Component, @Service and @Repository mark classes as beans; @Bean in a @Configuration class defines beans in code.

topics.name: Spring Boot Basics
topics.description: Starters, auto-configuration, application.properties and running a Boot application.
keyPoints: Starters (for example spring-boot-starter-web) bring a set of compatible dependencies.
Auto-configuration configures beans based on the classpath and your properties.
@SpringBootApplication enables component scanning and auto-configuration; settings live in application.properties or application.yml.

topics.name: REST Controllers
topics.description: @RestController, request mappings, path and query parameters, request bodies and responses.
keyPoints: @RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, so return values become the response body (as JSON).
@GetMapping and @PostMapping map URLs; @PathVariable reads /students/{id}, @RequestParam reads ?name= and @RequestBody reads the JSON body.
ResponseEntity lets you control the status code and headers.

topics.name: Spring Data JPA
topics.description: Entities, repositories, derived queries, relationships and transactions with JPA.
keyPoints: @Entity maps a class to a table and @Id marks the primary key.
A JpaRepository<T, ID> interface gives CRUD methods without writing implementations; derived queries such as findByEmail are generated from the method name.
@Transactional makes a method run in one transaction; lazy relationships load on first access.

topics.name: Validation & Error Handling
topics.description: Bean Validation annotations, @ControllerAdvice and consistent error responses.
keyPoints: Bean Validation annotations such as @NotBlank, @Size, @Email and @Min go on fields and are triggered by @Valid on the request body.
@ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler centralizes error handling for all controllers.
Return a consistent error body (status, message, field errors) with a proper status such as 400 or 404.

topics.name: Spring Security Basics
topics.description: Authentication vs authorization, password hashing and securing endpoints.
keyPoints: Authentication verifies who you are; authorization decides what you may do.
Never store plain-text passwords; hash them with a slow, salted algorithm such as BCrypt.
A SecurityFilterChain bean configures which endpoints need authentication or specific roles.

topics.name: Unit Testing with JUnit 5
topics.description: Writing tests, assertions, test lifecycle and parameterized tests.
keyPoints: A JUnit 5 test is a method annotated with @Test; it passes unless an assertion fails or an exception is thrown.
Common assertions: assertEquals(expected, actual), assertTrue and assertThrows.
@BeforeEach runs before every test; @ParameterizedTest runs one test with many inputs.

topics.name: Mocking with Mockito
topics.description: Mocks and stubs, verifying interactions and testing classes in isolation.
keyPoints: A mock replaces a real dependency so a class can be tested in isolation.
when(mock.method()).thenReturn(value) stubs behavior; verify(mock).method() checks that an interaction happened.
Mock collaborators such as repositories and clients, not the class under test or simple value objects.

topics.name: Testing Spring Boot Apps
topics.description: @SpringBootTest, MockMvc, test slices and testing REST endpoints.
keyPoints: @SpringBootTest starts the full application context; it is slow, so use it sparingly.
MockMvc sends simulated HTTP requests to controllers; @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer and @DataJpaTest only the persistence layer.
Use @MockBean (or @MockitoBean in newer Spring versions) to replace beans in a test slice.

topics.name: Big-O Notation
topics.description: Time and space complexity, common growth rates and best/worst/average case.
keyPoints: Big-O describes how running time or memory grows with the input size n, ignoring constant factors.
Common orders from fast to slow: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n).
Worst case is the usual default; best and average cases can differ (for example in quicksort).

topics.name: Analysing Loops & Recursion
topics.description: Counting operations in nested loops, recurrence relations and amortized cost.
keyPoints: A single loop up to n is O(n); two nested loops each up to n are O(n^2).
A loop that halves or doubles its variable every step runs O(log n) times.
Amortized cost averages expensive rare operations over many cheap ones, for example appending to a dynamic array is O(1) amortized.

topics.name: Arrays & Dynamic Arrays
topics.description: Indexing, insertion and deletion costs, and how dynamic arrays grow.
keyPoints: Arrays store elements contiguously, so access by index is O(1).
Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts elements, which costs O(n).
Dynamic arrays double their capacity when full, giving amortized O(1) appends.

topics.name: String Manipulation
topics.description: Character arrays, reversing, palindromes, anagrams and building strings efficiently.
keyPoints: Strings are often immutable, so repeated concatenation in a loop costs O(n^2); use a builder or a list of characters.
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards; check it with two pointers from both ends.
Two strings are anagrams if their character counts match.

topics.name: Two Pointers & Sliding Window
topics.description: Solving pair, subarray and substring problems in linear time.
keyPoints: Two pointers walk an array from both ends or at different speeds, avoiding nested loops.
A sliding window keeps a range [left, right] and updates its sum or counts as it moves, giving O(n).
In a sorted array, move the left pointer up if the sum is too small and the right pointer down if it is too large.

topics.name: Prefix Sums
topics.description: Precomputing running totals to answer range-sum queries in O(1).
keyPoints: prefix[i] stores the sum of the first i elements.
The sum of elements l..r is prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l], answered in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.
The same idea works for counts, XOR and 2-D grids.

topics.name: Linked Lists
topics.description: Singly and doubly linked lists, insertion, deletion, reversal and cycle detection.
keyPoints: Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node (and the previous node in a doubly linked list).
Inserting or deleting after a known node is O(1), but finding a node by index is O(n).
Floyd's cycle detection uses a slow and a fast pointer: if they meet, there is a cycle.

topics.name: Stacks
topics.description: LIFO operations, balanced brackets, expression evaluation and monotonic stacks.
keyPoints: A stack is last-in, first-out: push and pop at the top are both O(1).
Stacks check balanced brackets: push openers, and pop and match on closers.
A monotonic stack keeps elements in sorted order to find, for example, the next greater element in O(n).

topics.name: Queues & Deques
topics.description: FIFO operations, circular buffers and double-ended queues.
keyPoints: A queue is first-in, first-out: enqueue at the back and dequeue from the front.
A circular buffer reuses array slots with wrap-around indexes: (i + 1) % capacity.
A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends in O(1).

topics.name: Hash Tables
topics.description: Hash functions, collisions, hash maps and sets, and counting with maps.
keyPoints: A hash function maps a key to an array index; lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average.
Collisions (two keys with the same index) are handled by chaining or open addressing.
Use a map to count frequencies or to find a complement (two-sum) in one pass.

topics.name: Recursion Basics
topics.description: Base and recursive cases, the call stack and thinking recursively.
keyPoints: Every recursive function needs a base case that stops and a recursive case that moves toward it.
Each call is pushed onto the call stack; a missing base case causes a stack overflow.
Solve the smallest case first, then assume the function already works for smaller inputs.

topics.name: Binary Search
topics.description: Searching sorted data in O(log n) and binary search on the answer.
keyPoints: Binary search needs sorted data and halves the search range each step: O(log n).
Compute the middle as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 to avoid integer overflow.
Binary search on the answer finds the smallest value that satisfies a monotonic condition.

topics.name: Elementary Sorting
topics.description: Bubble, selection and insertion sort, stability and in-place sorting.
keyPoints: Bubble, selection and insertion sort are O(n^2) in the worst case.
Insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted data and is stable.
A stable sort keeps equal elements in their original order; an in-place sort uses O(1) extra space.

topics.name: Merge Sort & Quicksort
topics.description: Divide and conquer, merging, partitioning and O(n log n) sorting.
keyPoints: Merge sort splits the array, sorts the halves recursively and merges them: O(n log n) always, O(n) extra space, stable.
Quicksort partitions around a pivot: O(n log n) on average, O(n^2) in the worst case, and it sorts in place.
Both use divide and conquer.

topics.name: Backtracking
topics.description: Generating subsets and permutations, pruning, and N-Queens style problems.
keyPoints: Backtracking builds a solution step by step and undoes (backtracks) a choice when it cannot lead to a solution.
The template is: choose, explore recursively, un-choose.
Pruning impossible branches early (for example attacked squares in N-Queens) saves time.

topics.name: Binary Trees & Traversals
topics.description: Tree terminology, pre/in/post-order traversal and level-order traversal.
keyPoints: A binary tree node has at most two children; the top node is the root and nodes without children are leaves.
Pre-order visits root, left, right; in-order visits left, root, right; post-order visits left, right, root.
Level-order traversal uses a queue and visits nodes level by level.

topics.name: Binary Search Trees
topics.description: BST property, search, insert, delete and in-order successor.
keyPoints: In a BST every value in the left subtree is smaller and every value in the right subtree is larger than the node.
Search, insert and delete take O(h), where h is the height: O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed.
In-order traversal of a BST visits the values in sorted order.

topics.name: Heaps & Priority Queues
topics.description: Binary heaps, heapify, priority queues and top-k problems.
keyPoints: A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array where each parent is <= (min-heap) or >= (max-heap) its children.
Insert and remove-top are O(log n); peeking at the top is O(1); building a heap from n items is O(n).
A priority queue is usually a heap; keep a min-heap of size k to find the k largest elements.

topics.name: Tries
topics.description: Prefix trees for word storage, prefix search and autocomplete.
keyPoints: A trie stores strings character by character along paths from the root.
Insert, search and prefix checks cost O(L), where L is the word length, regardless of how many words are stored.
Tries power autocomplete and prefix search.

topics.name: Balanced Search Trees
topics.description: Why trees become unbalanced, rotations, and an overview of AVL and red-black trees.
keyPoints: Inserting sorted data into a plain BST creates a skewed tree with O(n) operations.
Balanced trees (AVL, red-black) keep the height O(log n) using rotations.
AVL trees are more strictly balanced; red-black trees do fewer rotations and are used in, for example, Java's TreeMap.

topics.name: Graph Representations
topics.description: Vertices and edges, directed vs undirected, adjacency lists and matrices.
keyPoints: A graph has vertices (nodes) and edges; edges may be directed or undirected and may carry weights.
An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbours: O(V + E) space, good for sparse graphs.
An adjacency matrix uses O(V^2) space but checks whether an edge u-v exists in O(1).

topics.name: BFS & DFS
topics.description: Breadth-first and depth-first search, connected components and grid traversal.
keyPoints: BFS explores level by level using a queue; DFS goes deep first using recursion or a stack.
Both run in O(V + E) with an adjacency list and need a visited set to avoid looping.
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS is useful for connected components and cycle detection.

topics.name: Topological Sort
topics.description: Ordering a DAG with Kahn's algorithm or DFS, and detecting cycles.
keyPoints: A topological order lists the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that every edge goes from an earlier to a later vertex.
Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes vertices with in-degree 0 using a queue.
If not all vertices get removed, the graph contains a cycle.

topics.name: Shortest Paths
topics.description: BFS on unweighted graphs and Dijkstra's algorithm on weighted graphs.
keyPoints: BFS gives shortest paths when all edges have the same weight.
Dijkstra's algorithm uses a min-priority queue and repeatedly settles the closest unsettled vertex; it needs non-negative weights.
Dijkstra runs in O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.

topics.name: Minimum Spanning Trees & Union-Find
topics.description: Disjoint-set union, Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms.
keyPoints: A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices of a weighted undirected graph with minimum total weight and no cycles.
Kruskal's algorithm sorts the edges and adds the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle, using union-find.
Union-find supports find and union in nearly O(1) with path compression and union by rank.

topics.name: Greedy Algorithms
topics.description: Greedy choice, interval scheduling and when greedy fails.
keyPoints: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders.
Interval scheduling: sort by end time and pick each interval that starts after the last chosen one ends.
Greedy fails for problems such as coin change with arbitrary coin values; use dynamic programming there.

topics.name: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
topics.description: Overlapping subproblems, memoization and bottom-up tabulation.
keyPoints: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.
Memoization is top-down: cache the results of recursive calls. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table in order.
Naive Fibonacci recursion is exponential; dynamic programming makes it O(n).

topics.name: 1-D Dynamic Programming
topics.description: Climbing stairs, house robber, coin change and longest increasing subsequence.
keyPoints: Define dp[i] clearly, for example the best answer using the first i items.
Climbing stairs: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]. House robber: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).
Coin change: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin]) over the coins; the standard LIS dynamic program is O(n^2).

topics.name: 2-D Dynamic Programming
topics.description: Grid paths, longest common subsequence, edit distance and 0/1 knapsack.
keyPoints: A 2-D table such as dp[i][j] often indexes prefixes of two strings or positions in a grid.
LCS: if the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; otherwise max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
0/1 knapsack: dp[i][w] = max(skip item i, take item i if it fits); edit distance takes the minimum of insert, delete and replace.
